newsitem.title: UK: Belfast police station hit, IRA suspected.
newsitem.headline: Belfast police station hit, IRA suspected.

text.p: Suspected nationalist guerrillas attacked a Belfast police station on Monday but no one was injured in what police believe was the IRA's latest attempt to kill a member of the Northern Ireland security forces.
Police said a device was thrown against the outside wall of the Pottinger police station in east Belfast in the Short Strand area, blowing out windows in nearby houses.
"I thought the house was going to come in on top of us." said mother of two Geraldine Forrester, who lives nearby.
It was thought to be the third attack by the Irish Republican Army guerrillas in three days in what police chiefs say is a deliberate strategy to kill a member of the security forces.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the incident, which bore all the hallmarks of the IRA's 1997 campaign.
The IRA, fighting to drive Britain from Northern Ireland and reunite the province with the Irish Republic, says that the 92 percent Protestant force is a tool of continued rule by London.

On Saturday night two mortars were fired harmlessly at a mobile police patrol in Downpatrick, 30 miles (50 km) southeast of Belfast and police also found a booby trap device set up to hit a police jeep near Londonderry, the province's second city.
Police believe Monday's attack was carried out using a so-called coffee jar bomb, a wad of explosives packed inside a small container which is hurled against its target.
The Downpatrick attack involved two of the IRA's home-made mortar bombs which were fired from a nearby ditch but passed over the police jeep and the car of a passing motorist.

Northern Ireland's police chief, Ronnie Flanagan, said on Sunday that IRA guerrillas appeared determined to kill members of his force in a rapidly escalating 1997 campaign which has raised fears of a return to total sectarian warfare.

The IRA ended a 17-month truce in February last year by bombing targets in Britain and a British army base in Germany in protest at the failure of its political wing, Sinn Fein, to win a seat at multi-party peace talks in Belfast.
No-one has been killed in Northern Ireland since the IRA returned to war in the province itself by bombing Britain's army base outside Belfast last October, killing one soldier.

But security forces fear that it is only a matter of time before the IRA kills a member of the 18,000-strong police force and its Protestant Loyalist adversaries respond by returning to tit-for-tat violence.
The Ulster Freedom Fighters, one outlawed Loyalist group, said last month that it would end its truce if the IRA killed anyone and police say they are taking the threat seriously.
Loyalists, who want Northern Ireland to remain British, called a truce in October 1994.
